# Does the Hype Fade?

### What ten years of BoardGameGeek data says about trusting launch ratings

*Draft v2, 2026-10-18. All numbers are generated by the pipeline (`reports/results/key_numbers.json`). Figures are in `reports/figures/`.*

---

## TL;DR

- The average new board game's rating on BoardGameGeek (BGG) **falls 0.40 points in its first three years**. **61%** of that drop comes in year one, and **87%** of games decline.
- The decline isn't finished at three years: **new raters still score games 0.23 below the displayed average**.
- **Hype doesn't decide how far a game falls; it decides how fast.** Heavily hyped games reach their lower rating within months; quiet releases take years.
- A rating becomes reliable (within ±0.25 of its 3-year value for 80% of games) at about **month 13**. A simple adjusted launch rating gets close to that by month 6.

---

## The question

Online ratings drive buying decisions, but a product's first raters are rarely typical. They're the fans, the backers and the people who preordered. Research on books and consumer goods shows early reviews tend to be more positive than later ones (Li & Hitt, 2008; Godes & Silva, 2012). Board-game players have their own name for this, the "cult of the new" (Booth, 2022). Studies that use BGG data still treat a game's rating as a fixed quality score.

So I asked three questions:

1. **How much, and how fast, do new games' ratings change after launch?**
2. **Do the most-hyped launches fall hardest?**
3. **When can you trust a new game's rating?**

## The data

[`beefsack/bgg-ranking-historicals`](https://github.com/beefsack/bgg-ranking-historicals) archives BGG's full ranked list every day since October 2016. I took one snapshot per month (121 snapshots, 2.6M rows) and followed **6,927 newly released games** that entered the ranking between January 2017 and October 2023, each for 36 months.

Building a clean panel took more care than expected, and these steps are where the analyst work was:

- **Truncated snapshots.** Two first-of-month files (Jan and Sep 2024) were partial scrapes missing ~3,500 games each. The pipeline checks row counts and substitutes the first complete file of the month.
- **Duplicate rows.** 721 games appear twice in the same daily file (ranks shift mid-scrape); these are deduplicated.
- **Junk metadata.** Publication years of 0 or 3000 would have mislabelled ancient games as 2021 releases.
- **Rounding.** BGG publishes averages to two decimals. That matters when you back out *what new raters think*: from two consecutive running averages, the average of just the ratings added in between is `(avg_t·n_t − avg_{t−1}·n_{t−1}) / (n_t − n_{t−1})`. For a game with 60,000 raters, rounding alone can swing that by ±6 points. I keep a value only when its worst-case rounding error is below 0.5 points.

The pipeline runs end to end with one command and checks itself against 36 automated quality checks. All of them pass.

## Finding 1: launch ratings oversell, and the correction is front-loaded

![Fig 1](figures/fig01_rating_change_by_age.png)

Measured from the month a game enters the ranking, its displayed average drops **0.24 points by month 12, 0.34 by month 24 and 0.40 by month 36**. That's a big move: it's two-thirds of the gap between a typical top-100 game and one ranked around 1,000th (median averages 7.9 vs 7.3 in October 2026). **87%** of games end lower than they started.

Is that just the whole site getting harsher? No. I tracked 2,428 established games over the same calendar months as a control group. They drifted only **−0.016**, so about 96% of the decline is specific to new releases.

## Finding 2: the decline isn't finished at three years

![Fig 2](figures/fig02_new_vs_displayed_gap.png)

Comparing *what new raters say* with *what's displayed*: new ratings come in about **0.15 points below the displayed average at month 3, and still 0.23 below at month 36**. The displayed number is a running average, so it carries the enthusiasm of the launch crowd long after that crowd stops rating. The result holds under every threshold combination I tested for the noisy new-rating estimate (gap −0.13 to −0.26).

## Finding 3: hype decides the speed, not the size

I expected the most-hyped games, the ones gaining raters fastest in their first six months, to fall furthest. **They don't.** Hype and the 3-year change are essentially uncorrelated (r = 0.01). Controlling for where a game started, more-hyped games fall *slightly less*. Measured only after the hype window, hype predicts nothing at all (coefficient −0.004, SE 0.013).

![Fig 9](figures/fig09_speed_not_size.png)

What hype does change is **timing**. By month six, the most-hyped quarter of games has already lost 0.19 points; the least-hyped quarter has lost 0.10. By month 36 they've converged (−0.41 vs −0.37). The mechanism is the running average itself. A game in the most-hyped quarter typically gains six times its launch raters within six months (median), which quickly dilutes the enthusiastic early ratings. For a game in the quietest quarter, the launch crowd still makes up 46% of its raters three years later, and its new raters score it 0.30 below the displayed number. **Quiet games aren't fading less; they just haven't finished fading.**

What does predict the size of the fall is **the starting rating**. Games entering around 8.8 lose 0.76 points on average; games entering around 5.8 lose 0.05. Part of this is statistical regression to the mean (launch averages rest on a median of just 34 ratings), and part is likely self-selection: the games that launch highest have the most devoted early audiences. This data can't fully separate the two.

![Fig 4](figures/fig04_change_distribution.png)

**Crowdfunding.** Matching 2017–2021 releases to a public Kaggle metadata set shows Kickstarter games fall further (−0.54 vs −0.36). Much of that is because they launch higher (7.62 vs 7.23), but even at the same starting rating they fall 0.05–0.16 more. This is consistent with backers being an especially self-selected first audience. It's descriptive only.

![Fig 10](figures/fig10_kickstarter.png)

## Finding 4: you can trust a rating after about a year, or adjust it sooner

![Fig 8](figures/fig08_when_to_trust.png)

At launch, only **31%** of games are within ±0.25 of their 3-year rating. That reaches 80% at **month 13**.

A platform doesn't have to wait that long. A three-variable model (displayed rating, number of raters, growth since launch), trained on 2017–2019 releases and tested on 2020–2023 releases, produces an **adjusted launch rating**. It is within ±0.25 of the eventual rating for **55%** of games at launch (vs 31%) and cuts the average error from 0.48 to 0.29. By month 6 it's within ±0.25 for 77% of games, nearly the 80% that raw ratings only reach at month 13. It works mainly by shrinking high launch ratings toward the typical level, which is exactly what the earlier findings suggest it should do.

One more twist: **74% of games climb in BGG's rank** while their raw average falls. The rank is based on a Bayes average that penalises games with few raters, so simply accumulating ratings lifts it. The number most users glance at goes up while actual opinion goes down.

## What a platform could do

1. **Label ratings younger than ~12 months** as "early" or "new release".
2. **Show an adjusted launch rating** alongside the raw one, or shrink early averages toward the category mean.
3. **Surface the recent-ratings average** next to the all-time one, as some app stores already do. It separates current opinion from launch enthusiasm.

The same playbook applies anywhere a running average meets a self-selected launch audience: app stores, e-commerce, streaming, restaurants.

## Limitations

- A game only enters the ranking at 30 ratings, so its very first ratings are folded into month 0. I measure change *after* entry.
- Observational data, so these are patterns, not causal effects. "Hype" (rater growth) also reflects print runs, distribution and price.
- The new-rater estimate is approximate (rounding, edited ratings) and is available for roughly half to two-thirds of game-months, more often for fast-growing games.
- One enthusiast platform. The Kickstarter flag comes from a 2022 snapshot and may be broader than "launched via crowdfunding".
- Monthly snapshots only; a daily-data robustness check is future work.

## How it's built

Python + DuckDB. The SQL pipeline (download → load → cohort → panel → QC) is driven by a single config file. The models are a game fixed-effects event study (`linearmodels`), cross-sectional OLS with robust SEs, game-level bootstrap CIs, a robustness grid with eight variants, and an out-of-sample predictive check.
